subject: maths
title: Expanding double brackets

slides.heading: Expanding double brackets — why it matters
slides.body: Expanding double brackets means multiplying every term in the first bracket by every term in the second to give a three-term quadratic. This is the step that connects factorised form to expanded form — two different ways of writing the same expression. You'll need it every time you work with quadratics, whether solving equations, sketching curves, or completing the square.
slides.note: Maximum 3 sentences. Plain English. No AQA references. What is this and why does it matter.

slides.heading: The FOIL / grid method
slides.formula: (a + b)(c + d) = ac + ad + bc + bd
slides.formulaExplained: FOIL is a memory aid: First (a × c), Outer (a × d), Inner (b × c), Last (b × d). Always four products. A grid with the two terms from the first bracket as column headers and the two from the second as row headers gives the same four cells. After expanding, collect the two middle terms to simplify.
slides.whenToUse: Any time you see two pairs of brackets multiplied together — in quadratic equations, area problems, and any simplification question involving two linear factors.
slides.note: Show formula in standard notation. Explain each variable. State when this formula applies.

slides.heading: Let's work through one
slides.question: Expand and simplify (2x + 1)(x − 5).

steps.instruction: First: multiply the first terms. 2x × x = 2x².
Last: 1 × (−5) = −5. Then collect like terms: −10x + x = −9x.

slides.note: Numbers must differ from any question in the question bank for this subtopic.

slides.heading: Watch out for this

mistakes.mistake: Only doing two multiplications — e.g. (2x + 1)(x − 5) = 2x² − 5, missing both middle terms entirely.
mistakes.correction: FOIL gives four products. The middle two (outer and inner) combine into the x-term: −10x + x = −9x. Skipping them means losing the middle term of the quadratic.

mistakes.mistake: Collecting middle terms with the wrong sign — e.g. writing −10x + x = −11x instead of −9x.
mistakes.correction: −10x + (+1x) = −9x. The +1 comes from the Inner step: 1 × x = +x. Keep the sign with the term.

mistakes.mistake: Treating (a + b)² as a² + b² — e.g. (x + 4)² = x² + 16, omitting the 2ab middle term.
mistakes.correction: (x + 4)² = (x + 4)(x + 4). Use FOIL: x² + 4x + 4x + 16 = x² + 8x + 16. The middle term 2ab = 2 × x × 4 = 8x is always present.

slides.note: Minimum 2, maximum 3 mistakes. Specific not generic.

keyFacts.fact: (a + b)(c + d) = ac + ad + bc + bd — always four products. FOIL: First, Outer, Inner, Last.
keyFacts.examTip: Count your terms before collecting: you should have four products before any simplifying. If you only have two, you've missed steps.

keyFacts.fact: (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b² — the perfect square always has a middle term 2ab. It is never just a² + b².
keyFacts.examTip: (x + 5)² = x² + 10x + 25. The 10x is 2 × x × 5. This is an extremely common exam error.

keyFacts.fact: (a + b)(a − b) = a² − b² — difference of two squares. The middle terms cancel: +ab and −ab sum to zero.
keyFacts.examTip: Recognise the pattern: same terms, opposite signs in each bracket. Result has no x-term: (x + 7)(x − 7) = x² − 49.
